strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: using corrections collected during interactive segmentation to improve a deployed model under distribution shift.
The proposed two-stage adaptation procedure is simple and computationally attractive, requiring only two backpropagation updates per image compared with ten or more for the reported baselines.

The evaluation covers multiple fundus and brain MRI datasets, including modality and pathology shifts, and the method produces consistent gains over the frozen model and prior continuous-adaptation approaches. Improvements are especially substantial for BRATS T1/T1c and ATLAS.
The ablations provide useful evidence that the two stages play complementary roles and that the Gaussian Point Loss improves performance as more images are processed.
The method, motivation, and experimental findings are generally presented clearly, and the same base interactive model is used for the main adaptation-method comparisons.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies entirely on simulated, ground-truth-aware clicks. No real-user study or robustness analysis covers inaccurate, inconsistent, or alternative clicking behavior, weakening claims about clinical practicality.

The sequential evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified for an order-sensitive online method. Image ordering, shuffling, initialization across datasets, and the number of random trials are unclear; most brain results have no variance or statistical significance estimates.

The brain MRI evaluation retains only the slice with the largest total lesion area from each 3D case and merges lesion labels. This substantially simplifies the clinical task and limits the strength of claims about adaptation across MRI pathologies.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Only two continuous interactive-adaptation methods are compared consistently, while the MedSAM Adapter comparison is poorly contextualized and does not establish a controlled backbone- or compute-matched comparison. Image-specific fine-tuning and broader test-time/online adaptation baselines are absent.

Ablations are confined largely to one fundus cup dataset. There is no sensitivity analysis for the consequential GPL weight, Gaussian width, spatial window, learning rate, or number of adaptation clicks, and the effect of using GPL during initial base-model training is not isolated.

The method distills a ten-click prediction into future predictions, creating a risk of confirmation errors and drift. The paper does not evaluate nonstationary streams, adverse ordering, long-term stability, or retention when the distribution changes again.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is only promised, and important implementation details such as update-step configuration, point encoding, preprocessing, image resolution, sequence construction, and handling of empty/error components are missing.

The private TBI dataset is described minimally, without acquisition details, access information, ethics approval, or consent discussion. Overall, the results are promising, but these evaluation and reporting gaps leave the submission slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: using interaction-derived feedback for continuous post-deployment adaptation under distribution shift.
The two-stage procedure is simple and intuitively motivated: it distills a many-click prediction into a one-click prediction and separately trains responsiveness to correction clicks.

Experiments cover several public fundus and brain MRI datasets, multiple modalities and pathologies, and generally show sizable improvements over the shared frozen model and the TSCA/IA+SA baselines, especially for one-click performance under large shifts.

Using the same ISFCNN initialization for the principal continuous-adaptation methods improves the fairness of those comparisons, and the component ablation provides some evidence that both stages and GPL contribute.
weaknesses: The contribution appears technically incremental for a top-tier AI venue. GPL is essentially spatially Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy around clicks, while the adaptation procedure is self-training from a many-click prediction; the manuscript does not clearly establish a substantial conceptual advance over prior correction-based online adaptation.

The evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous to support the broad reliability and clinical-practicality claims. Clicks are simulated using ground-truth error regions, there is no evaluation with clinicians or realistic noisy/suboptimal interactions, and every image receives up to ten oracle-like corrections.

Results can depend strongly on online sample order, random click placement, and initialization, but the ordering protocol, seeds, variability, and statistical significance are largely absent. Only selected methods are said to be averaged over three runs, without standard deviations or confidence intervals.

The brain MRI evaluation retains only the single 2D slice with the largest lesion area from each 3D case. This excludes small-lesion, empty-slice, and volumetric behavior and can substantially overstate clinical segmentation performance. Only Dice is reported, with no boundary or lesion-wise metrics.

Baseline coverage is narrow: the main comparisons use an older FCNN backbone and only two continuous interactive-adaptation methods. The isolated MedSAM Adapter comparison is not clearly matched in training, interaction capability, parameter count, or adaptation budget, and stronger modern interactive segmentation models are not evaluated.

The ablation is limited to one fundus target dataset. It does not study sensitivity to beta, sigma, learning rate, click budget, pseudo-label quality, sequence ordering, or distribution-shift severity. It is also unclear whether removing GPL refers only to online adaptation or to base-model training, where GPL is also used.

The method may reinforce erroneous final predictions through self-training. The claim that regions unaffected by clicks preserve general segmentation ability is asserted rather than demonstrated, and there is no analysis of error accumulation, calibration, failure cases, or long-horizon stability.

Practical-efficiency claims are unsupported by wall-clock time, memory use, hardware measurements, or comparison of total computation. Requiring ten interactions on every image may itself be a substantial clinical burden.

Reproducibility and ethics reporting are incomplete: preprocessing, architecture details, data-stream construction, and several implementation choices are missing; code is only promised after publication; and the private TBI dataset lacks acquisition, cohort, consent/IRB, demographic, and access information. strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important problem: exploiting routine interactive corrections to continuously adapt medical-image segmentation models under post-deployment distribution shift.

The proposed two-stage procedure is simple and computationally attractive. It explicitly improves both one-click localization and response to subsequent correction clicks, requiring only two backpropagation steps per image versus substantially more for the reported baselines.

The evaluation is broad, covering five fundus datasets and four brain MRI datasets, with challenging shifts across institutions, modalities, and pathologies. OAIMS produces particularly large improvements for BRATS T1/T1c and ATLAS, while retaining performance on the in-distribution FLAIR setting.

Comparisons use a shared base interactive model and favorable learning rates for competing adaptation methods, improving fairness. The paper also reports results at multiple click budgets, a reduced-click experiment, and component ablations that generally support the proposed design.
weaknesses: All interactions are simulated using ground-truth error regions. There is no clinician study or robustness analysis for imperfect, inconsistent, or differently placed clicks, leaving uncertainty about whether the gains transfer to real interactive workflows.

The baseline set is narrow. The main comparisons are against IA+SA and TSCA using an older ISFCNN backbone; Medical SAM Adapter is evaluated only in one setting and is not an online-adaptation method. Results across additional modern interactive architectures and relevant test-time or online-adaptation baselines would better establish generality.

Statistical evidence is incomplete: only some fundus results are said to be averaged over three runs, no standard deviations or significance tests are reported, and the MRI results appear to use single runs. Online adaptation can be sensitive to sample ordering, but order sensitivity is not studied.

The brain evaluation uses only the single 2D slice with the largest lesion area from each case. This substantially simplifies the clinical task and limits conclusions about full-volume or routine 3D segmentation performance.

Ablations are confined to G1020 cup segmentation and do not include sensitivity analyses for GPL parameters, learning rate, click count, or adaptation order. There is also little analysis of drift, failure cases, or long-horizon behavior.

Reproducibility and clinical governance need strengthening: code is only promised, important preprocessing and sequence-construction details are limited, the TBI dataset is private, and the manuscript does not state ethics approval or data-governance information for that institutional cohort.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: continuously adapting interactive medical-image segmentation systems under scanner, modality, and pathology shifts.

The proposed combination of post-interaction and mid-interaction adaptation is simple, computationally lightweight, and produces large improvements over IA+SA and TSCA, particularly for difficult MRI shifts.

The empirical study is broad, spanning five fundus datasets and four brain-MRI datasets, with modality and pathology shifts, mixed-domain streams, reduced click budgets, noisy clicks, and source-domain return experiments.
Component and loss-design ablations generally support the value of the post-interaction stage, mid-interaction stage, Gaussian weighting, and class-restricted local loss.
The paper is understandable and provides useful algorithmic descriptions, latency measurements, and a clicks-to-target-Dice evaluation.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies entirely on an oracle simulator that inspects ground-truth masks and clicks the largest erroneous component. There is no clinician study or analysis with realistic human click placement, so claims about clinical practicality and user efficiency are stronger than the evidence.

Most tables report only point estimates. Except for one small ablation, there are no confidence intervals, seed-level variation, or statistical tests. Results from sequential adaptation can depend substantially on image order and random click placement, but this variability is inadequately characterized.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the manuscript omits essential details such as optimizer and learning rates for each adaptation stage, preprocessing and resizing, training schedules, exact U-Net configuration, dataset split sizes for several targets, image ordering, and target-domain validation procedures. Code is only promised after publication.

Hyperparameters are said to come from preliminary experiments, while the appendix evaluates them on target datasets, but the paper does not clearly separate target validation data from reported test data. This leaves a risk of test-set-informed selection.

The novelty is moderate: the method mainly combines self-training on interaction-refined predictions with a Gaussian-weighted local cross-entropy term. The comparison set is narrow for a test-time/domain-adaptation contribution, covering only IA+SA and TSCA as adaptive baselines and using Med-SA only as a frozen model.

The mid-interaction optimization is technically ambiguous. Algorithm 1 marks the new-click prediction as having no gradient and then defines a loss between stored consecutive predictions, without specifying graph retention or recomputation of the pre-click prediction. The exact gradient path—and therefore a reproducible implementation of this central component—is unclear.

The MRI evaluation selects only the single 2D slice with the largest lesion per case and merges lesion classes. This substantially narrows the clinical task, avoids full-volume consistency and many difficult or empty slices, and limits the generality of conclusions about medical segmentation.

The method assumes the final model-produced mask is sufficiently accurate once the user is satisfied, but users never directly provide a corrected mask. Synthetic noisy-click tests do not fully address systematic pseudo-label errors, calibration, or silent failure in actual deployment. Ethical and safety limitations of continually updating a clinical model are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: adapting interactive medical-image segmentation models to distribution shifts using corrections naturally produced during deployment.
The proposed post- and mid-interaction adaptation framework is simple and computationally inexpensive, and the click-centered Gaussian loss is intuitive.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering multiple fundus datasets, MRI modalities, and brain pathologies. Reported improvements over ICNN, IA+SA, and TSCA are often large, particularly for severe MRI shifts.

The paper includes useful component ablations, latency measurements, reduced-click experiments, source-domain checks, and stress tests involving mixed domains, poor pseudo-labels, and erroneous clicks.
weaknesses: The mid-interaction algorithm is not technically specified in a reproducible way. Algorithm 1 marks the new-click prediction used as the pseudo-target as requiring no gradient, while the optimized prediction is a previously generated output. It does not state the differentiable recomputation needed to update the current parameters; taken literally, the described update has no valid current computation graph.

The online evaluation is highly dependent on the target-image sequence, yet the main experiments do not report sequence construction, multiple orderings, variability across seeds, or confidence intervals. Averaging performance over an adapting test stream can conceal poor cold-start behavior and makes the very large one-click gains difficult to assess rigorously.

Most reported results appear to be single runs, despite stochastic click placement and sequential adaptation. There are no statistical tests or uncertainty estimates, and some nominally corresponding results differ slightly across tables.

The evaluation uses ground-truth masks to simulate localization and corrective clicks, always targeting erroneous connected components. There is no clinician study or realistic interaction-noise study, so conclusions about smooth clinical workflows and user efficiency are substantially stronger than the evidence.

The MRI evaluation uses only the 2D slice with the largest lesion from each 3D case. This removes small-lesion, empty-slice, and volumetric-consistency challenges and considerably weakens the claimed medical and clinical significance.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript omits essential training and adaptation details such as optimizer settings, learning rates, preprocessing, image resolution, most dataset splits and sequence sizes, stopping/thresholding choices, and baseline-specific tuning. Code and models are only promised after publication.

The core novelty is limited. Dense self-training on a user-refined prediction and Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy around clicks are straightforward extensions of prior online interactive segmentation, while comparisons against recent test-time adaptation and broader interactive adaptation methods are limited.

The non-public TBI dataset is insufficiently documented, including cohort size, acquisition details, split construction, and ethics or consent information. This prevents reproduction and leaves an ethical-reporting concern for a clinically framed paper.

Claims of model agnosticism, applicability to scribbles and other prompts, resistance to forgetting, and transformative clinical potential are not directly validated. Overall, the promising numerical results do not overcome the methodological ambiguity, fragile evaluation protocol, and reproducibility gaps required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: continuously adapting interactive medical-image segmentation systems using feedback already produced during routine interaction.

The combination of post-interaction adaptation, mid-interaction adaptation, and the Click-Centered Gaussian loss is intuitive, computationally lightweight, and sufficiently distinct from prior sparse-click adaptation methods.

The empirical results are broad and compelling: experiments span five fundus datasets, four brain-MRI datasets, modality and pathology shifts, fewer-click regimes, mixed-domain streams, extreme shifts, and erroneous clicks. Improvements over IA+SA and TSCA are particularly large on difficult MRI transfers.

The component ablations, CCG design ablations, hyperparameter analysis, source-domain checks, click-efficiency experiment, latency measurements, and qualitative examples provide useful support for the main conclusions.
The method is clearly motivated and described, with equations and pseudocode that make the high-level procedure understandable.
weaknesses: All interactions are simulated using ground-truth masks: correction clicks target the largest erroneous component, and the selected MRI slice is the slice with the largest lesion. This gives the evaluation access to information unavailable in deployment and leaves the central claim of practical clinician-guided adaptation unvalidated by real users or realistically noisy interaction trajectories.

Main results generally report only mean Dice without confidence intervals, per-case distributions, significance tests, or variability across image order and random seeds. This is especially consequential for sequential online learning, where results can depend strongly on stream order; only one limited ablation explicitly averages three runs.

The experimental setup omits important reproducibility details, including dataset sizes and splits for most targets, preprocessing and augmentation, optimizer and adaptation learning rates, and several training settings. The code and pretrained models are only promised for future release.

Evaluation uses one 2D slice per 3D MRI case and binary merging of lesion classes. This substantially simplifies realistic volumetric medical segmentation and limits the strength of the clinical-practicality claims.

The strongest comparisons use an older U-Net-style interactive backbone. Med-SA is included but frozen and performs poorly, so the study does not establish whether the adaptation mechanism retains its advantages with strong contemporary foundation-model or transformer-based interactive segmenters.

The method assumes the final user-refined prediction is suitable as a pseudo-label, but there is no explicit acceptance or quality-control mechanism. Robustness experiments are encouraging, yet they do not characterize long-horizon drift across multiple deployment sites or systematic annotation biases.

Claims about a smooth real-world or clinical workflow are stronger than the evidence: there is no clinician study, end-to-end interaction-time evaluation, or discussion of governance and safeguards for continually updating a deployed medical model.
